claim: Variable impedance/admittance control and learning strategies can support compliant human–robot physical interaction, but safe effectiveness depends on sensing quality, task and user conditions, controller assumptions, and explicit stability/passivity safeguards.
claim_locator: Controller-supplied full-text packet: definition and taxonomy of variable impedance control
Controller-supplied full-text packet: learning strategies and challenges
epistemic_status: Author-reported survey synthesis; no independent verification or causal superiority claim inferred.
problem_and_setting: Physical human–robot interaction requiring online adjustment of desired inertia, damping, and stiffness to balance compliance/transparency, movement accuracy, and stability amid uncertain human and environmental dynamics.
method_or_mechanism: A systematic taxonomy of impedance/admittance variation and learning methods: velocity-, force-, and EMG-based adaptation; neural/adaptive and optimal-control schemes; Gaussian mixture/regression and dynamic movement primitive representations; reinforcement learning; and demonstration- or EMG-informed approaches. Stability considerations include Lyapunov analysis, passivity/energy reasoning, and constraints on time-varying gains.
content_summary: The survey reviews roughly two decades of methods for varying or learning impedance/admittance during HRI. It distinguishes signal modalities and their trade-offs: velocity approaches can avoid force sensing but need task-specific calibration; force-based approaches regulate interaction force but require reliable force measurements; EMG-based approaches estimate intent or limb impedance but require wearable acquisition, processing, and robustness across subjects. It emphasizes that stability guarantees are architecture- and assumption-specific, and identifies safe adaptation, sensing reliability, generalization, and integration of learning with formal guarantees as unresolved challenges.
synthesis_role: Background and taxonomy source for framing design alternatives, sensing requirements, safety constraints, and unresolved research gaps in adaptive impedance control for HRI.
development_link: Supports development of an adaptive-HRI harness by motivating explicit representation of sensing modality, task/user calibration, controller architecture, and stability/passivity assumptions as first-class evaluation conditions rather than treating learned impedance adaptation as universally safe or superior.

evidence.locator: Controller-supplied full-text packet: variable impedance definition and modality taxonomy
evidence.finding: Variable impedance control modulates desired inertia, damping, and stiffness online; velocity-, force-, and EMG-based approaches have distinct sensing and calibration trade-offs.
Lyapunov, passivity/energy, and time-varying-gain constraints are discussed, but validity of a stability result depends on the modeled system, sensing, architecture, and assumptions.

evidence.locator: Controller-supplied full-text packet: learning and challenges sections
evidence.finding: Learning routes span adaptive/neural, optimal-control, GMM/GMR, DMP, reinforcement-learning, and demonstration/EMG-informed methods; open issues include safe adaptation, reliable sensing, and generalization.

boundary_conditions: Physical HRI with online impedance/admittance adaptation.
Conclusions are survey-level and do not establish superiority of any individual method.
Stability claims are conditional on exact dynamics, sensing, controller design, and stated assumptions.
Performance and usability may vary by task, motion regime, user, and environment.
assumptions: Desired impedance parameters can be meaningfully estimated or updated online.
Required position, force, and/or EMG signals are available with sufficient quality for the selected method.
Controller and robot/human/environment models satisfy conditions required by any invoked Lyapunov, passivity, or optimal-control analysis.
Calibration and robustness procedures are adequate for task and user variability.

reported: Velocity-based approaches can be task- and calibration-dependent.
Force-based approaches require reliable interaction-force information.
EMG-based approaches require wearable acquisition, signal processing, and subject-specific robustness.
Safe stable adaptation, generalization, and integration of learning with formal stability/passivity constraints remain challenges.
inferred: A deployment that omits sensing-quality checks or stability/passivity constraints may adapt impedance unsafely under unmodeled human or environmental dynamics.
Treating this survey as experimental proof of a method's superiority would overstate its evidence.

verification_status: Grounded only in the supplied controller packet; bibliographic and full-text claims not independently checked.
